name: Rotating the List Values to the Right by One Position
description: Construct a program that has a function that receives a list of values and returns the list rotated to the right by one position so that the value that is currently at the end of the list is moved to the front, shifting the remaining values to the right. For example, if the list is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], the program will change it to [6, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5].
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def rotate_right(lst):
    #Step 1.1: Store the value at the end of the list in a local variable
    last = lst[len(lst)-1]
    #Step 1.2: Rotate the remaining values of the list to the right 
    for i in range(len(lst)-1, 0, -1):
        lst[i] = lst[i - 1]
    #Step 1.3: Move the value at the end to the front of the list
    lst[0] = last
    return lst
#Step 2: Call the function
values = [3, 8, 9, 8, 7, 5]
print("Original list:", values)
print("Rotated list: ", rotate_right(values))

comments.content:
We need to first declare the function so that we can call it later. The following lines declare the function rotate_right that takes a list, rotates the list to the right by one position, and returns the rotated list.

Note that all statements following the header line are indented.

The value at the end of the list is supposed to go to the front of the list, and the other values are supposed to rotate backward. We can make the task easier by storing the value at the end of the list into a local variable and then shift the other values to the right by one position.

This statement stores the value at the end of the list that is located at the index len(lst)-1 in the variable last. We will use variable last later to move the value at the end to the front of the list.
The function call len(lst) returns the number of the values in the list.

With value at the end safely tucked away, we now have to shift the remaining values to the right by one position. We could break down the overall task into shifting operations, each of which is a simple assignment statement. Because of repeated shift operations on the list values, we’d want to write this with a for loop. We’ll replace the value at index i with the value currently stored at index i-1, this will shift the value at index i-1 to the right, by one position.

To properly shift the values to the right, we have to run the loop in reverse order (from right to left instead of left to right). We need to use the range function to get a sequence of list indexes in the reverse order, starting at the last index and going down to 0 (exclusive).

We get this sequence by calling the function range(len(lst)-1, 0, -1). The reason that we do not want to include the index 0 is that in the assignment statement in the loop body we always move the value one position before the current index. That is, when we get into index 1 in the sequence, we move the value at index 0 to index 1.
Note that len(lst) returns the number of the values in the list. Also note that all statements inside the loop need to be indented with respect to the loop header.
We need to shift value at index i-1 to value at index i. We do this by setting the value at index i to the value at index i-1.

After shifting the values to the right, we’ve made room at the front of the list for the value that used to be at the end of the list (which is currently stored in a local variable called last). This statement copies the value of variable last to the index 0 in the list.
Note that 0 is the index of the first value in the list.
Now that we finished rotating the list values, we need to return the rotated list. The return statement, when reached, ends the function call and sends the result back to the caller.
We define the list referred by variable values to hold specified numbers. We initialize the list by separating values with a comma and enclosing the collection in square brackets [ ].

This statement prints to the default standard output stream the text "Original list:" followed by the content of the list.
The printed text shows the arguments of the print function separated by the default delimiter (i.e., single space character) and followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
Note that we can see the content of the list by calling the print function and passing the list to that.

This statement prints to the default standard output stream the text "Rotated list: " followed by the content of the list returned from the function call.

Note that any changes that were made to the list within the rotate_right function affect the original list in the calling function. That is, after the function call, the list referred by variables values will be changed to the rotated list.
Note that we do not necessarily have to store the returned list from the function call in a variable. We could use the list returned from the function call directly in the print function.
The function call must be done after the function is declared. Also note that we can see the content of the list by calling the print function and passing the list to that.
